subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: 'Vertical integration' of a media company means that the company:
options: Controls several stages of production and distribution within one medium
Is owned by the state
Owns several different types of media (e.g. press and TV)
Merges with a non-media business
questions.explain: Vertical integration is the ownership of different stages of the same production and distribution chain (e.g. a film studio owning cinemas).

questions.q: The Glasgow University Media Group is best associated with which approach to the media?
options: Uses and gratifications
The hypodermic syringe model
The hegemonic/neo-Marxist dominant-ideology approach
Pluralism
questions.explain: The GUMG's content analysis argued news embodies a dominant ideology through journalists' shared assumptions rather than conspiracy.

questions.q: Research on media representations of ethnicity has frequently found that minority ethnic groups are:
options: Over-represented as professionals and experts
Associated disproportionately with problems such as crime, conflict or immigration
Always shown positively
Entirely absent from all media
questions.explain: Studies show minority ethnic groups are often stereotyped and linked to threats or problems, while being under-represented in everyday positive roles.

questions.q: Stuart Hall's reception (encoding/decoding) model proposes that audiences can adopt which readings of a media text?
options: Only the preferred reading
Preferred, negotiated or oppositional readings
No readings at all
Hypodermic readings only
questions.explain: Hall argued audiences decode messages in dominant/preferred, negotiated, or oppositional ways depending on their social position.

questions.q: The concept of 'deviancy amplification' suggests that media coverage can:
options: Only affect elite groups
Reduce the amount of deviance in society
Increase the deviance it reports by sensationalising and labelling it
Have no relationship to deviance
questions.explain: Deviancy amplification describes how media reaction can magnify and even produce more of the deviance it highlights, often via a self-fulfilling prophecy.

questions.q: Katz and Lazarsfeld's 'two-step flow' model argues that media messages:
options: Are always rejected by audiences
Are mediated by opinion leaders who interpret and pass them on to others
Have no effect on the audience
Reach all audience members directly and identically
questions.explain: The two-step flow model holds that opinion leaders receive and interpret media content before influencing the wider audience.

questions.q: Neophiliacs (optimists) about the new media argue that it:
options: Widens choice, participation and access to information, enhancing democracy
Increases owner control and passivity
Inevitably creates moral panics
Has no social effects
questions.explain: Neophiliacs see new media as empowering, expanding consumer choice, participation and democratic engagement.

questions.q: Pluralists respond to claims of owner bias by arguing that owners' influence is limited by:
options: The hypodermic syringe effect
Market forces, journalistic autonomy, the law and the need to attract audiences
A single dominant ideology
Government nationalisation of all media
questions.explain: Pluralists argue competition, professional norms, legal regulation and audience demand constrain what owners can dictate.

questions.q: Cultural pessimists about the new media argue that it:
options: Removed commercial influence from the media
Reinforces existing inequalities (the digital divide) and concentration of ownership
Has democratised access for everyone equally
Eliminated all media bias
questions.explain: Pessimists argue new media deepen inequalities through the digital divide and remain dominated by powerful commercial interests.

questions.q: Which term describes the editorial 'sifting' process by which only some events are selected to become news?
options: Norm-setting
Two-step flow
Agenda-setting
Gatekeeping
questions.explain: Gatekeeping refers to editors and journalists controlling which stories pass through to become news.

questions.q: The 'hypodermic syringe' model of media effects assumes that:
options: Audiences use media to satisfy their own needs
Audiences actively interpret media in varied ways
Effects are filtered through opinion leaders
The media inject messages directly into a passive audience, producing immediate effects
questions.explain: The hypodermic model treats audiences as passive and assumes media messages have a direct, uniform and powerful effect.

questions.q: Postmodernists such as Baudrillard argue that in the media-saturated world we increasingly live in a state of:
options: Absolute poverty
Hegemonic class consciousness
Hyperreality, where media simulations blur the line between image and reality
Pure pluralism of ownership
questions.explain: Baudrillard's hyperreality describes a condition in which media simulations (simulacra) become more 'real' than reality itself.

questions.q: Which trend best describes the pattern of media ownership over recent decades?
options: The disappearance of private media companies
Growing concentration into a small number of large transnational conglomerates
Increasing fragmentation into many small independent firms
Complete state ownership of all media
questions.explain: Ownership has become increasingly concentrated and globalised, with a few transnational conglomerates dominating across platforms.

questions.q: Stuart Hall et al.'s 'Policing the Crisis' analysed the moral panic over 'mugging' as serving to:
options: Divert attention from the crisis of capitalism by scapegoating young black men
Reflect genuine consumer demand for crime news
Empower ethnic minority audiences
Demonstrate pluralist diversity
questions.explain: Hall argued the mugging panic functioned ideologically to legitimate increased control during a crisis and shifted blame onto a racialised folk devil.

questions.q: In media studies, the 'digital divide' refers to:
options: The split between print and broadcast media
The gap between fact and opinion online
Inequalities in access to and use of new media and the internet
The division of media ownership between firms
questions.explain: The digital divide describes unequal access to digital technology, often along lines of class, age, region and global inequality.

questions.q: The term 'cultural imperialism' in media globalisation refers to:
options: The export of Western, especially American, media and culture overwhelming local cultures
State censorship of foreign media
The growth of local media in developing nations
Equal exchange of culture between all nations
questions.explain: Cultural imperialism describes the dominance of powerful (largely Western) media exporting their values and eroding indigenous cultures.

questions.q: The concept of 'narrowcasting' refers to:
options: Broadcasting to the entire mass population
State control of broadcasting
The decline of all media
Targeting media content at specific, segmented audiences
questions.explain: Narrowcasting describes the targeting of niche, segmented audiences, a feature of new and digital media, in contrast to mass broadcasting.

questions.q: 'News values' are best defined as:
options: The criteria journalists use to judge whether an event is newsworthy
The profit margins of news organisations
The political opinions of media owners
The ethical code of journalism
questions.explain: News values (e.g. immediacy, negativity, personalisation, elite persons) are the implicit criteria by which events are selected and prioritised as news.

questions.q: The concept of 'citizen journalism' associated with new media refers to:
options: State-controlled reporting
Journalism produced only by professionals
Advertising-funded broadcasting
Members of the public creating and sharing news content via digital technology
questions.explain: Citizen journalism describes ordinary people using digital tools to gather, report and distribute news, challenging traditional gatekeeping.

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognised news value identified by Galtung and Ruge?
options: Random selection
Audience boredom
Negativity (bad news)
Owner indifference
questions.explain: Galtung and Ruge listed values such as negativity, threshold, unexpectedness and reference to elite nations and persons.

questions.q: The 'symbolic annihilation' of women in the media (Tuchman) refers to their being:
options: Shown only as professionals
Over-represented in positions of power
Omitted, trivialised or condemned in media representations
Represented identically to men
questions.explain: Symbolic annihilation describes the absence, trivialisation or condemnation of women in media content, reflecting and reinforcing their subordination.

questions.q: The pluralist theory of media ownership and content holds that:
options: The media transmit a single dominant ideology
Media content is shaped largely by consumer demand and a diversity of competing views
Owners dictate all media content directly
Journalists impose ruling-class hegemony
questions.explain: Pluralists argue that in a competitive market the media give audiences what they want and reflect a plurality of opinions.

questions.q: In Stanley Cohen's work, a 'folk devil' is:
options: An opinion leader in the two-step flow
A group defined as a threat to societal values, becoming a focus of public concern
A measure of audience ratings
A media owner who manipulates the news
questions.explain: Cohen described folk devils as the deviant groups (e.g. mods and rockers) demonised by the media during a moral panic.

questions.q: Older people, particularly older women, are frequently represented in the media through:
options: Constant association with power and authority
Negative or limited stereotypes such as being a burden, frail or out of touch
Complete invisibility in advertising only
A wide and varied range of active roles
questions.explain: Studies note older people are often stereotyped negatively, with older women especially marginalised compared with older men.

questions.q: A 'moral panic', as theorised by Stanley Cohen, involves:
options: Audiences ignoring a social problem
A purely economic crisis in the media industry
Exaggerated media reaction to a group, amplifying deviance and prompting calls for control
A gradual, balanced media discussion of an issue
questions.explain: Cohen's study of mods and rockers showed how media exaggeration creates disproportionate public concern and can amplify the very deviance it condemns.

questions.q: The 'uses and gratifications' model views the audience as:
options: Active users who select media to satisfy needs such as information, identity and entertainment
Determined entirely by owners
Helpless victims of moral panics
Passive recipients of injected messages
questions.explain: Uses and gratifications (Blumler and McQuail) sees audiences actively choosing media to meet personal needs.

questions.q: Laura Mulvey's concept of the 'male gaze' refers to media representations that:
options: Position the audience to view women as objects of heterosexual male desire
Ignore gender entirely
Empower female audiences
Show men as victims
questions.explain: The male gaze describes how visual media frame women as objects to be looked at from a masculine, heterosexual viewpoint.

questions.q: The hegemonic (dominant-ideology) approach, drawing on Gramsci, differs from instrumental Marxism by arguing that ruling-class dominance in the media is:
options: Driven entirely by audience preferences
Impossible in modern media systems
An unintended outcome of journalists' shared, taken-for-granted middle-class worldview
The result of deliberate owner instruction
questions.explain: Hegemonic/neo-Marxist writers (e.g. the GUMG) see bias as arising not from direct orders but from journalists' largely unconscious consensus assumptions.

questions.q: 'Agenda-setting' by the media means that the media:
options: Tell audiences exactly what to think
Have no effect on public opinion
Always reflect the public's existing priorities
Influence what issues people think about by deciding what to cover
questions.explain: Agenda-setting suggests the media shape which topics are seen as important, even if they do not determine opinions on them.

questions.q: The manipulative (instrumental) Marxist view of media ownership argues that:
options: Owners directly use the media to transmit ruling-class ideology and propaganda
Media content reflects audience demand in a free market
Media output reflects the everyday assumptions of journalists
The media empower diverse competing groups
questions.explain: Instrumental Marxists, such as Miliband, see owners deliberately using their control to disseminate ideas that serve ruling-class interests.
